summary:
Kazakhstan decriminalised consensual sex between men in late 1997, when Article 104 of the Penal Code, which criminalised "buggery", was repealed; the repeal took effect in 1998 and introduced a common age of consent of 16. Sex between women was never a criminal offence. The sources record no statute regulating clothing by gender presentation and no law restricting which toilet or facility a trans visitor may use.

A statutory ban on "propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation" is the operative legal threat. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the law on 30 December 2025, prohibiting "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and in the media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. Kazakhstan now stands with Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting such material by statute. An earlier legislative threat preceded this: in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed it was reviewing a petition titled "We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!" from the Union of Parents, which had met the threshold for government consideration.

Trans visitors should expect document scrutiny. Since 2003, transgender people in Kazakhstan may change legal gender on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder" involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge. Although since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty, because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to begin medical transition. Since 2011, document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation; people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. A passport or ID that does not match presentation may therefore be common, and mismatched documents are a realistic screening risk.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or form civil unions in Kazakhstan, and such couples and households headed by them are not eligible to the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. As of 2020 same-sex couples could not legally adopt; in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a "key role" in approval, assessed through a "special psychological test". Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation.

No laws protect LGBTQ people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit. A 2015-16 Pew survey found 89% of people opposed same-sex marriage. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review for January–December 2023 documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over, with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022. ECOM, which has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017, identifies health-right barriers in Kazakhstan alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.

On 24 September 2019 Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, upholding privacy rights over a "moral foundations" defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety. The most recent documented incident of this kind in the record is from 2019; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE/ODIHR since the 2018 report and has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes; ODIHR's 2024 reporting notes the country would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures. Bias-motivated violence is therefore documented but not systematically recorded by the state.

The 2025 propaganda law places Kazakhstan alongside Russia, Hungary and Georgia in prohibiting "LGBTQ propaganda" by statute, a regional pattern that may shape how border and cultural officials treat visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no region-specific signal for Kazakhstan's sub-national units beyond the Almaty medical commission's practical monopoly on gender-marker changes; the national assessment applies.

Whether the 2025 propaganda law has been enforced against any individual, and how, is not sourced in this inventory; the penalty structure (10-day arrest and fine) is documented but no enforcement case is.

The inventory does not document airport or border screening practices specific to transgender travellers in Kazakhstan; no differential treatment claim can be made from these sources.
